deep.reconstruction:
The page determines the wire intervals ('Fadenweite') of a transit or meridian instrument reticle at Göttingen, April–May 1818. The next page contains clock corrections from star transits over the same dates. Two intervals (two columns, probably two thread distances or the means of two halves of the reticle) are expressed in seconds of time for a star on the equator.

(A) Polaris and a second circumpolar star. The slow transit of Polaris across the wires was timed. Since t_obs = F·sec δ, the reduction F = t_obs·cos δ (cos δ ≈ 0.029 for δ ≈ 88°21' in 1818) gives the equatorial interval F. The tabulated values are already reduced.
- Col. 1: Apr 20 16.360, Apr 26 16.463, May 1 16.547, [λ?] Ursae 16.358, May 8 16.392, [λ?] Ursae 16.498, May 9 16.378.
- An extra entry 'May 8 [?]' gives 16.413.
- Col. 2: 16.248, 16.235, 16.025, 16.170, 16.043, 16.087, 16.145.
- The 'Ursae' entries are presumably the other close-polar star λ (or δ) Ursae Minoris, used in the same way.
- No mean is written. My computation: the col. 1 mean is ≈16.428 and the col. 2 mean is ≈16.136.

(B) 'Andre Sterne' (other stars), Apr 20. For seven stars the raw intervals t_i (seconds of time) are listed for both wire intervals, together with s_i = sec δ_i:
- κ Cas: 35.0, 33.9; s = 2.1245
- β Cas: 31.0, 31.1; s = 1.8947
- η Cas: 29.9, 30.0; s = 1.8284
- Sirius: 17.4, 16.4; s = 1.0428
- Regulus: 17.0, 16.9; s = 1.0257
- Spica: 16.8, 16.3; s = 1.0161
- γ Vir: 16.9, 16.0; s = 1.0000

The declinations implied by these secants match the 1818 positions:
- Sirius −16°29'
- Regulus +12°53'
- Spica −10°11'
- γ Vir ≈ −0°27'
- η Cas ≈ +56°50'
- β Cas ≈ +58°08'
- 2.1245 implies δ ≈ 61°55'. This is κ Cas in 1818, not α Cas (55°31', sec 1.766).

The model is t_i = F·s_i. Gauss estimates F by the ratio of sums, F = Σt_i / Σs_i:
- Σt = 164.0 and 160.6; Σs = 9.9322.
- F = 164.0/9.9322 = 16.512 s and 160.6/9.9322 = 16.170 s.

These agree reasonably with the Polaris results, closely for col. 2 and about 0.08 s higher for col. 1. The pencil '1306' at the foot is probably an archival or library number.
errors: No arithmetic errors: all three column sums (164.0, 160.6, 9.9322) and both quotients (16.512, 16.170) check.
The star labelled with a Greek letter read as 'α Cassiop.' must be κ Cassiopeiae: sec δ = 2.1245 implies δ ≈ 61.9°, which fits κ Cas in 1818, not α Cas (sec ≈ 1.77). The handwritten κ resembles an x.

The ratio estimator Σt/Σsecδ is not the least-squares estimate (Σt·s/Σs²) under equal errors in t. It is a legitimate weighted mean, but it is not optimal if timing errors are independent of δ. This is a methodological remark, not an error.

results.what: Determination of the equatorial wire interval of a transit instrument from transit times of stars at various declinations, reducing by sec δ (t = F sec δ), including circumpolar stars (Polaris).
results.modern_name: Reduction of wire (thread) intervals to the equator in transit-instrument practice
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th–19th c. practical astronomy (Bradley, Tobias Mayer, Bessel and others)

results.what: Combining several stars by F = Σt_i / Σ sec δ_i
results.modern_name: Ratio estimator / weighted mean with weights proportional to sec δ

deep.surprise_reason: This is routine observatory reduction work (thread-interval determination) from Gauss's Göttingen observing notebooks of 1818. It is fully standard practice with no new mathematics.

checkable.asserts: ≈ 61.92°, the declination of κ Cas in 1818 (not α Cas)

transcription_corrections: First star in 'Andre Sterne' is κ Cassiop. (written like 'x'), not α Cassiop., as confirmed by sec δ = 2.1245.
'l Ursae' is probably λ (possibly δ) Ursae [Minoris], a close-polar star.
The '²' after 16"360 is likely a stray mark or footnote sign, not an exponent.
'May 8 Anon[?]' is uncertain, possibly 'May 8 Anm.' or a similar note; the value is 16.413.
'1306' at the foot is a later pencil archival number, not part of the computation.
